input.question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?
input.ground_truth: Venus’ day is 243 earth days long. Magellan orbited Venus every 3 hours or so. That means that during a single Venusian day, the probe circled the planet almost 2000 times. I don’t know what you mean by quickly, but it took almost an entire earth year to get that 96%, for what it’s worth.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?

response.prediction:
Sure! Here’s how I’d explain it to a 5-year-old:

Imagine Venus is like a big, cloudy cake that you can’t see inside. NASA wanted to see what the cake looks like underneath the clouds, so they sent a special robot spaceship called Magellan to visit Venus.

Magellan flew around Venus many times, like a bird flying in circles above the cake. As it flew, it used special eyes (called radar) that can see through clouds. These eyes bounced invisible beams off the cake (Venus’s surface) and came back to the spaceship. Magellan used these bounced beams to draw a picture of what the cake’s surface looks like.

Because Magellan went around Venus a lot and used its special eyes all the time, it was able to draw a very good map of Venus really fast!
